blindSummary:
A 1984 equal-opportunity statute here protects a "gender history" attribute, defined in binary, medically-inflected terms (a person who identifies as, and lives or seeks to live as, the opposite sex). This is a narrower formulation than the "gender identity" language used in several other states/provinces and in the federal anti-discrimination statute: a non-binary or gender-nonconforming visitor may not meet the state/provincial definition and would rely solely on federal coverage for a state/provincial complaint. This state/province has no state anti-vilification offence (civil or criminal) and no statutory charter of rights binding public authorities.

Reform is underway: a 2024 amendment to the law registering sex and gender changes received assent in September 2024, removing medical and surgical prerequisites for registration, with substantive commencement by proclamation. This will feed back into the scope of the protected attribute for complaints purposes but was not yet fully in force at the time of writing.

Against the country-wide baseline, this state/province sits slightly below it: the narrower protective vocabulary and the absence of both a vilification offence and a rights charter mean the state/provincial safety net is thinner than in several other states/provinces, even though the federal floor is unchanged. Compared with a neighbouring state/province, which has a 2019 human-rights statute binding public authorities and a conversion-practice prohibition in force since 2020, this state/province lacks both the structural review mechanism and the specific coercion safeguard.
